title: Pre-Unit 1 · Review
note: Hand-authored review lesson covering the WHOLE of Pre-Unit 1 (district Pre-Unit: Course 1 Pre Unit, Aug 24 - Sep 8) - all six 'Math Is...' lessons 1-1 through 1-6 and the four Grade 5 review standards they carry: 5.NF.B.4 (fractions of a whole number), 5.NBT.B.7 (decimal operations), 5.MD.C.5 (volume of rectangular prisms) and 5.OA.B.3 (patterns and rules). Its id is deliberately not of the form <unit>-<lesson>, so it stays outside the numbered lesson spine, district pacing and scope-and-sequence by id shape - the same way 6-1-6-2-practice does. Every problem restates content from one of the six lessons; nothing here teaches anything Pre-Unit 1 did not.
contentObjective: I can use everything Pre-Unit 1 taught — estimating with reasoning, fractions of a whole number, decimal operations, volume of a rectangular prism, and pattern rules — and explain which one a problem is asking for.
languageObjective: I can explain my thinking using the words estimate, strategy, representation, argument, pattern rule and critique.

vocabulary.definition: A reasoned answer that is close enough to be useful, worked out instead of counting everything.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una respuesta razonada, suficientemente cerca para ser útil, que se calcula en vez de contarlo todo.
vocabulary.example: About 20 cars with about 4 riders each is about 80 riders.
vocabulary.visual: Count one handful you CAN count, then ask how many handfuls fill the jar.

vocabulary.definition: The plan you choose for solving a problem — draw a model, write an equation, or build a table.
vocabulary.definitionEs: El plan que eliges para resolver un problema: dibujar un modelo, escribir una ecuación o hacer una tabla.
vocabulary.example: For 3/4 of 20 chairs, the plan was: find one fourth first, then take three of them.
vocabulary.visual: Name what you know, name what you are looking for, then pick the plan.

vocabulary.definition: A picture, table, or diagram that shows the quantities in a problem and how they are related.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Un dibujo, tabla o diagrama que muestra las cantidades de un problema y cómo se relacionan.
vocabulary.example: A tape diagram shows $7.50 split into 3 equal parts of $2.50.
vocabulary.visual: Label every part and unit, then read the numbers straight off the picture.

vocabulary.definition: A claim backed by mathematics that somebody else can check for themselves.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una afirmación respaldada con matemáticas que otra persona puede comprobar por si misma.
vocabulary.example: "Two jumbo boxes hold 800 cubic inches and three large boxes hold 720, so buy the jumbo boxes."
vocabulary.visual: State the claim, show the calculation, name the units.

vocabulary.definition: The rule that connects every input to its output, so you can predict a term you have not reached.
vocabulary.definitionEs: La regla que conecta cada entrada con su salida, para poder predecir un término al que no has llegado.
vocabulary.example: 1 to 5, 2 to 10, 3 to 15 — the rule is multiply by 5, so 7 gives 35.
vocabulary.visual: A rule has to work on EVERY row of the table, not just the row you checked.

vocabulary.definition: To examine someone's reasoning and say exactly where it works or where it breaks.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Examinar el razonamiento de alguien y decir exactamente donde funciona o donde falla.
vocabulary.example: "One fourth of 24 is not 3 — the fraction stayed the same but the whole doubled, so the amount doubles too."
vocabulary.visual: Point at the step that breaks, not at the person.

questions.stem: Pre-Unit 1 kept asking you to ESTIMATE instead of counting everything. What makes an answer a good estimate?
choices: It is reasoned from something you counted, and close enough to be useful
It is a guess you make quickly without thinking
It is always a round number
choiceFeedback: A guess has no reasoning behind it. An estimate can be explained and checked.
Estimates are often round, but that is a side effect. What makes it good is the reasoning.
If it were exactly right it would be a count, not an estimate.
questions.explanation: Across Lessons 1-1, 1-2 and 1-3 the routine was the same: find a group you CAN count, then work out how many of those groups there are. An estimate is a reasoned answer that is close enough to be useful.
hints: Think about the peas, the coins and the Ferris wheel. What did all three have in common?
In each one you counted a small group first.
Then you asked how many of those groups fill the whole thing.
questions.stemEs: La Pre-Unidad 1 te pedía ESTIMAR en vez de contar todo. ¿Qué hace que una respuesta sea una buena estimación?
choicesEs: Esta razonada a partir de algo que contaste y esta suficientemente cerca para ser útil
Es una adivinanza rápida sin pensar
questions.explanationEs: En las Lecciones 1-1, 1-2 y 1-3 la rutina fue la misma: encuentra un grupo que SÍ puedas contar y calcula cuántos de esos grupos hay.
hintsEs: Piensa en los chícharos, las monedas y la rueda de la fortuna. ¿Que tenían en común?
En cada uno contaste primero un grupo pequeño.
Luego preguntaste cuántos de esos grupos llenan el total.

questions.stem: Which unit belongs on a VOLUME answer?
choiceFeedback: Square units measure a flat surface, like a tabletop. A box holds space, not just surface.
Plain inches measure length in one direction. Volume uses all three directions at once.
Pounds measure weight. Two boxes can weigh the same and hold different amounts.
questions.explanation: Volume measures the space inside a solid, and space is filled with cubes — so volume answers carry cubic units. Lesson 1-4 asked you to defend a recommendation with accurate units, and this is the unit it meant.
hints: Volume is about the space INSIDE, not the surface or the length.
What shape fills a space perfectly with no gaps?
Cubes fill space, so the unit is cubic.
questions.stemEs: ¿Qué unidad corresponde a una respuesta de VOLUMEN?
questions.explanationEs: El volumen mide el espacio dentro de un sólido, y el espacio se llena con cubos, así que las respuestas de volumen llevan unidades cúbicas.
hintsEs: El volumen es el espacio de ADENTRO, no la superficie ni el largo.
¿Que figura llena un espacio sin dejar huecos?
Los cubos llenan el espacio, así que la unidad es cúbica.

questions.stem: You find a pattern rule that works for the first two numbers you check. What does Lesson 1-5 say you should do next?
choices: Test it on more terms — a rule has to work every time to be a rule
Change the rule so it fits only those two numbers
Start the pattern over with different numbers
choiceFeedback: Two matches can happen by accident. The third term is where most wrong rules fall apart.
A rule that only fits the numbers you already have predicts nothing new.
The pattern is fine. What needs testing is your rule about it.
questions.explanation: A generalization is a claim about EVERY term, so two matches are not enough to earn it. Lesson 1-5 asks you to organise the values in a table and check the rule connects every input to its output.
hints: A rule is a promise about every term, not just the ones you looked at.
What is the cheapest way to find out if the promise holds?
Put the values in a table and check the next term.
questions.stemEs: Encuentras una regla de patrón que funciona con los dos primeros números que revisas. ¿Qué dice la Lección 1-5 que debes hacer después?
choicesEs: Probarla con mas términos: una regla tiene que funcionar siempre para ser una regla
Cambiar la regla para que solo sirva con esos dos números
Empezar el patrón de nuevo con otros números
questions.explanationEs: Una generalización es una afirmación sobre CADA término, así que dos coincidencias no bastan. Organiza los valores en una tabla y comprueba la regla.
hintsEs: Una regla es una promesa sobre cada término, no solo los que miraste.
¿Cuál es la forma mas barata de saber si la promesa se cumple?
Pon los valores en una tabla y comprueba el siguiente término.

reviewHighlights.title: The five moves Pre-Unit 1 taught
reviewHighlights.rule: Pre-Unit 1 was not five separate topics — it was one habit practised five ways: figure out what the problem is asking for, choose a representation, do the mathematics, and be able to explain why the answer is reasonable.
steps: ESTIMATE (Lessons 1-1, 1-2, 1-3): find a group you can count, then work out how many of those groups there are.
A FRACTION OF A NUMBER (Lesson 1-2): “of” means multiply — find one part first, then take as many parts as you need.
DECIMALS (Lesson 1-3): equal groups multiply and equal shares divide, then check the answer back the other way.
VOLUME (Lesson 1-4): length × width × height, and the answer is in CUBIC units because it fills space.
PATTERNS (Lesson 1-5): put the values in a table, find the rule that works on EVERY row, then predict a term you have not reached.
reviewHighlights.watchOut: The most common Pre-Unit 1 mistake is reporting an estimate as if it were exact. 15 stacks of about 10 coins is about 150 coins — the multiplication is exact, but both numbers going in were estimates, so the answer is too. The second most common is the unit: a volume answer is in cubic units, never square units.
reviewHighlights.example: Lesson 1-4's box problem, start to finish: one large box is 8 × 3 × 10 = 240 cubic inches, so three hold 720. One jumbo box is 10 × 4 × 10 = 400 cubic inches, so two hold 800. 800 is greater than 720, so for the same price the jumbo boxes give 80 cubic inches more cereal.

revealWordProblem.title: Tonight's Problem: The Cereal Aisle
revealWordProblem.text:
Three large cereal boxes cost the same as two jumbo boxes. A large box is 8 inches long, 3 inches wide and 10 inches tall. A jumbo box is 10 inches long, 4 inches wide and 10 inches tall.

Question: which should you buy, and what is your argument?

level1.stem: A jar is full of marbles — too many to count one at a time. You count one small handful: about 10 marbles. About 8 handfuls fill the jar. About how many marbles are in the jar?
choiceFeedback: That adds the two numbers. Each handful has 10 marbles, and there are 8 of them — that is groups, so multiply.
That subtracts. The jar holds many handfuls, so the answer must be much larger than one handful.
That is 8 x 100. Each handful is about 10, not 100.
level1.explanation: Estimating means finding a group you CAN count, then asking how many of those groups there are. 8 handfuls of about 10 is 8 x 10 = 80.
hints: What can you actually count here — the whole jar, or one handful?
8 handfuls, 10 marbles in each. That is 8 equal groups.
8 groups of 10 is 8 x 10.
level1.stemEs: Un frasco esta lleno de canicas: son demasiadas para contarlas una por una. Cuentas un puñado pequeño: unas 10 canicas. Unos 8 puñados llenan el frasco. ¿Aproximadamente, cuántas canicas hay en el frasco?
level1.explanationEs: Estimar es encontrar un grupo que SÍ puedes contar y luego preguntar cuántos de esos grupos hay. 8 puñados de unas 10 son 8 x 10 = 80.
hintsEs: ¿Qué puedes contar de verdad aquí: el frasco entero o un puñado?
8 puñados, 10 canicas en cada uno. Son 8 grupos iguales.
8 grupos de 10 son 8 x 10.

level1.stem: Three fourths of the 20 chairs in the room are taken. How many chairs are taken?
choiceFeedback: That is one fourth of 20 — the chairs that are still empty. The question asks for the three fourths that are taken.
That adds 20 and 3. 'Three fourths of' is multiplication, not addition.
That multiplies 20 by 4. A fraction of a number is smaller than the number, not larger.
level1.explanation: Three fourths OF a number means multiply: 3/4 x 20. One fourth of 20 is 5, so three fourths is 3 x 5 = 15 chairs.
hints: 'Of' a number, with a fraction in front of it, means multiply.
Start with one fourth: 20 divided into 4 equal parts.
One fourth of 20 is 5. You need three of those fourths.
level1.stemEs: Tres cuartos de las 20 sillas del salón están ocupadas. ¿Cuántas sillas están ocupadas?
level1.explanationEs: Tres cuartos DE un número significa multiplicar: 3/4 x 20. Un cuarto de 20 es 5, así que tres cuartos son 3 x 5 = 15 sillas.
hintsEs: 'De' un número, con una fracción delante, significa multiplicar.
Empieza con un cuarto: 20 repartido en 4 partes iguales.
Un cuarto de 20 es 5. Necesitas tres de esos cuartos.

level1.stem: A notebook costs $1.25. You buy 4 notebooks. What is the total cost?
choiceFeedback: That adds 4 to the price of one notebook. You are buying 4 notebooks, so it is 4 groups of $1.25.
That is $1.25 more than the right answer — it adds one notebook too many.
That divides $1.25 by 4. Dividing would give the price of a PART of one notebook.
level1.explanation: Four notebooks at the same price is 4 groups of $1.25, so multiply: 1.25 x 4 = 5.00. Four quarters make a dollar, so four $1.25 notebooks make $5.00 exactly.
hints: Are you buying one notebook or four? Four equal prices is four equal groups.
Think in quarters: $1.25 is five quarters, and four times five quarters is twenty quarters.
level1.stemEs: Un cuaderno cuesta $1.25. Compras 4 cuadernos. ¿Cuál es el costo total?
level1.explanationEs: Cuatro cuadernos al mismo precio son 4 grupos de $1.25, así que multiplica: 1.25 x 4 = 5.00.
hintsEs: ¿Compras uno o cuatro? Cuatro precios iguales son cuatro grupos iguales.
Piensa en monedas de 25: $1.25 son cinco monedas de 25, y cuatro veces cinco son veinte.

level1.stem: A box is 5 inches long, 2 inches wide, and 3 inches tall. What is its volume?
choiceFeedback: That is 5 x 2 — only the bottom layer. The box is 3 inches tall, so there are 3 of those layers.
The number is right but the unit is not. Square inches measure a flat surface; a box holds space, so the unit is CUBIC inches.
That doubles the answer. Multiply the three measurements once each: 5 x 2 x 3.
level1.explanation: Volume of a rectangular box is length x width x height: 5 x 2 x 3 = 30. Volume fills SPACE, so the unit is cubic inches.
hints: Volume asks how much space is inside, so all three measurements matter.
Find the bottom layer first: 5 x 2.
The bottom layer is 10 cubic inches, and the box is 3 layers tall.
level1.stemEs: Una caja mide 5 pulgadas de largo, 2 de ancho y 3 de alto. ¿Cuál es su volumen?
level1.explanationEs: El volumen de una caja rectangular es largo x ancho x alto: 5 x 2 x 3 = 30. El volumen llena ESPACIO, así que la unidad es pulgadas cúbicas.
hintsEs: El volumen pregunta cuánto espacio hay adentro, así que importan las tres medidas.
Encuentra primero la capa de abajo: 5 x 2.
La capa de abajo es 10 pulgadas cúbicas y la caja tiene 3 capas.

level1.stem: A pattern starts at 3 and follows the rule ADD 4: 3, 7, 11, 15, ... What is the next number?
choiceFeedback: That adds 3, the STARTING number, instead of 4, the rule.
That adds 5. Check the jump between terms: 3 to 7 is 4, and 7 to 11 is 4.
That adds 1. The rule tells you exactly how much to add each step.
level1.explanation: The rule is add 4 every step, so the pattern grows by the same amount each time. 15 + 4 = 19.
hints: What is the jump from one number to the next? Check it twice.
3 to 7 is a jump of 4, and 7 to 11 is a jump of 4 too.
The last number shown is 15, and the rule says add 4.
level1.stemEs: Un patrón empieza en 3 y sigue la regla SUMAR 4: 3, 7, 11, 15, ... ¿Cuál es el siguiente número?
level1.explanationEs: La regla es sumar 4 en cada paso, así que el patrón crece la misma cantidad cada vez. 15 + 4 = 19.
hintsEs: ¿Cuál es el salto de un número al siguiente? Compruébalo dos veces.
De 3 a 7 hay un salto de 4, y de 7 a 11 también.
El último número mostrado es 15 y la regla dice sumar 4.

level1.stem: Two students explain the same answer. Which one has made a mathematical ARGUMENT?
choices: "Two jumbo boxes hold 800 cubic inches and three large boxes hold 720, so the jumbo boxes hold more."
"The jumbo boxes are better because I like them more."
"The jumbo boxes, because they look bigger."
"The jumbo boxes. Everyone in my group said so."
choiceFeedback: A preference is not evidence. An argument has to give a reason someone else can check.
How something looks can be misleading, and it gives the reader no numbers to check.
Agreement is not evidence. An argument stands on the mathematics, not on how many people said it.
level1.explanation: An argument states a claim and backs it with mathematics somebody else can check. The first one gives both totals and compares them, so a reader can redo the calculation and see for themselves.
hints: An argument gives a reason someone else could check for themselves.
Which explanation contains numbers a reader could recompute?
Look for the one that states BOTH totals and then compares them.
level1.stemEs: Dos estudiantes explican la misma respuesta. ¿Cuál de ellos ha construido un ARGUMENTO matemático?
choicesEs: "Dos cajas jumbo tienen 800 pulgadas cúbicas y tres cajas grandes tienen 720, así que las jumbo tienen más."
"Las cajas jumbo son mejores porque me gustan más."
"Las jumbo, porque se ven más grandes."
"Las jumbo. Todos en mi grupo lo dijeron."
level1.explanationEs: Un argumento da una afirmación y la respalda con matemáticas que otra persona puede revisar. El primero da los dos totales y los compara.
hintsEs: Un argumento da una razón que otra persona puede comprobar.
¿Cuál explicación tiene números que un lector podría volver a calcular?
Busca el que dice LOS DOS totales y luego los compara.

level2.stem: A Ferris wheel has 20 cars, and about 4 people fit in each car. About how many people can ride at one time?
choiceFeedback: That adds the cars and the riders. Each car holds 4 people and there are 20 cars — that is 20 equal groups.
That divides 20 by 4. Dividing would tell you how many cars each person gets.
That subtracts. More cars means MORE riders, so the answer must be bigger than 20.
level2.explanation: This is the estimate from Lesson 1-1. Count what you can (20 cars), estimate the rest (about 4 riders each), then multiply: 20 x 4 = 80. An estimate is a reasoned answer that is close enough to be useful.
hints: How many equal groups are there, and how big is each group?
20 cars, about 4 riders in each car.
20 groups of 4 is 20 x 4.
level2.stemEs: Una rueda de la fortuna tiene 20 cabinas y en cada una caben unas 4 personas. ¿Aproximadamente, cuántas personas pueden subir a la vez?
level2.explanationEs: Cuenta lo que puedes contar (20 cabinas), estima el resto (unas 4 personas por cabina) y multiplica: 20 x 4 = 80.
hintsEs: ¿Cuántos grupos iguales hay y que tan grande es cada grupo?
20 cabinas, unas 4 personas en cada cabina.
20 grupos de 4 son 20 x 4.

level2.stem: Two thirds of the 18 students in a group finished early. How many students finished early?
choiceFeedback: That is ONE third of 18 — the students still working. The question asks for the two thirds who finished.
That multiplies 18 by 3 divided by 2. A fraction less than 1, times a number, gives LESS than the number.
That is half of 18. Two thirds is more than half, so the answer must be greater than 9.
level2.explanation: Two thirds OF 18 means 2/3 x 18. One third of 18 is 6, so two thirds is 2 x 6 = 12 students.
hints: Find one third first: 18 split into 3 equal groups.
One third of 18 is 6.
You need TWO of those thirds: 2 x 6.
level2.stemEs: Dos tercios de los 18 estudiantes de un grupo terminaron temprano. ¿Cuántos estudiantes terminaron temprano?
level2.explanationEs: Dos tercios DE 18 significa 2/3 x 18. Un tercio de 18 es 6, así que dos tercios son 2 x 6 = 12 estudiantes.
hintsEs: Encuentra primero un tercio: 18 repartido en 3 grupos iguales.
Un tercio de 18 es 6.
Necesitas DOS de esos tercios: 2 x 6.

level2.stem: Three tickets cost $7.50 altogether. All three tickets cost the same. What does ONE ticket cost?
choiceFeedback: That subtracts 3 from $7.50. Splitting a total into equal shares is division, not subtraction.
That multiplies by 3. Multiplying makes the amount bigger, but one ticket costs LESS than all three.
That misplaces the digits. 7.50 divided by 3 gives 2 dollars and 50 cents, not 2 dollars and 5 cents.
level2.explanation: Equal shares means divide: 7.50 divided by 3 = 2.50. Check it back the other way — 2.50 x 3 = 7.50.
hints: Is one ticket more or less than the total for three?
Equal shares out of a total is division: 7.50 divided by 3.
Split $7.50 into 3 equal parts, then check by multiplying your answer by 3.
level2.stemEs: Tres boletos cuestan $7.50 en total. Los tres cuestan lo mismo. ¿Cuánto cuesta UN boleto?
level2.explanationEs: Partes iguales significa dividir: 7.50 entre 3 = 2.50. Comprueba al revés: 2.50 x 3 = 7.50.
hintsEs: ¿Un boleto cuesta más o menos que el total de tres?
Partes iguales de un total es división: 7.50 entre 3.
Reparte $7.50 en 3 partes iguales y luego comprueba multiplicando por 3.

level2.stem: A large cereal box is 8 inches long, 3 inches wide, and 10 inches tall. How much cereal do THREE large boxes hold in total?
choiceFeedback: That is the volume of ONE box. The question asks about three of them.
That adds the three measurements. Volume multiplies them: 8 x 3 x 10.
That is only 8 x 10 — it leaves out the width.
level2.explanation: This is the box problem from Lesson 1-4. One box is 8 x 3 x 10 = 240 cubic inches, and three boxes hold 240 x 3 = 720 cubic inches.
hints: Find one box first, then deal with the three.
One box: length x width x height = 8 x 3 x 10.
One box is 240 cubic inches, and there are 3 boxes.
level2.stemEs: Una caja grande de cereal mide 8 pulgadas de largo, 3 de ancho y 10 de alto. ¿Cuánto cereal caben TRES cajas grandes en total?
level2.explanationEs: Una caja es 8 x 3 x 10 = 240 pulgadas cúbicas, y tres cajas tienen 240 x 3 = 720 pulgadas cúbicas.
hintsEs: Encuentra primero una caja y luego ocupate de las tres.
Una caja: largo x ancho x alto = 8 x 3 x 10.
Una caja son 240 pulgadas cúbicas, y hay 3 cajas.

level2.stem: A table of values pairs each input with an output:  1 -> 5,  2 -> 10,  3 -> 15. What is the output when the input is 7?
choiceFeedback: That is the output for an input of 4. The question asks about an input of 7.
That adds 5 to 7. Check the rule against the whole table: 1 -> 5 is not 1 + 5 = 6.
That is 6 x 5. Multiply the input you were asked about, which is 7.
level2.explanation: Read the table for the rule that connects EVERY input to its output: each output is the input times 5. So the rule is multiply by 5, and 7 x 5 = 35.
hints: Compare each input with its own output. What happens to 1 to make 5?
1 x 5 = 5, 2 x 5 = 10, 3 x 5 = 15 — the same rule works on every row.
The rule is multiply by 5, and the input is 7.
level2.stemEs: Una tabla de valores empareja cada entrada con una salida:  1 -> 5,  2 -> 10,  3 -> 15. ¿Cuál es la salida cuando la entrada es 7?
level2.explanationEs: Busca la regla que conecta CADA entrada con su salida: cada salida es la entrada por 5. La regla es multiplicar por 5, y 7 x 5 = 35.
hintsEs: Compara cada entrada con su propia salida. ¿Qué le pasa al 1 para llegar a 5?
1 x 5 = 5, 2 x 5 = 10, 3 x 5 = 15 — la misma regla sirve en cada fila.
La regla es multiplicar por 5 y la entrada es 7.

level2.stem: A classmate says: "One fourth of 12 is 3, so one fourth of 24 must also be 3, because it is still one fourth." What should you say back?
choices: "One fourth of a BIGGER whole is a bigger amount — one fourth of 24 is 6."
"You are right, one fourth is always 3."
"One fourth of 24 is 3 because 24 divided by 8 is 3."
choiceFeedback: The fraction stayed the same but the whole doubled, so the amount doubles too.
That divides by 8 instead of 4. One fourth means 4 equal parts.
Fractions work with any whole number. The mistake is about the size of the whole, not about 24.
level2.explanation: Critiquing reasoning means finding exactly where it breaks. The fraction is the same, but the WHOLE is not: one fourth of 12 is 3 and one fourth of 24 is 6. A fraction always names a part OF something, so the whole matters.
hints: Did the fraction change, or did the thing you are taking a fraction OF change?
One fourth of 12 is 12 split into 4 groups. Now split 24 into 4 groups.
24 split into 4 equal groups gives 6, not 3.
level2.stemEs: Un compañero dice: "Un cuarto de 12 es 3, así que un cuarto de 24 también debe ser 3, porque sigue siendo un cuarto.¿" Qué le responderías?
choicesEs: "Un cuarto de un entero MÁS GRANDE es una cantidad más grande: un cuarto de 24 es 6."
"Un cuarto de 24 es 3 porque 24 entre 8 es 3."
"Las fracciones no se pueden usar con 24."
level2.explanationEs: Criticar un razonamiento es encontrar exactamente donde falla. La fracción es la misma, pero el ENTERO no: un cuarto de 12 es 3 y un cuarto de 24 es 6.
hintsEs: ¿Cambió la fracción, o cambio aquello DE lo que tomas la fracción?
Un cuarto de 12 es 12 repartido en 4 grupos. Ahora reparte 24 en 4 grupos.
24 repartido en 4 grupos iguales da 6, no 3.

level3.stem: A large cereal box is 8 by 3 by 10 inches and a jumbo box is 10 by 4 by 10 inches. Three large boxes cost the same as two jumbo boxes. Which choice gives MORE cereal, and by how much?
choices: Two jumbo boxes, by 80 cubic inches
Three large boxes, by 80 cubic inches
They give exactly the same amount
Two jumbo boxes, by 160 cubic inches
choiceFeedback: The totals are right but compared backwards: 800 is greater than 720, so the jumbo boxes give more.
720 and 800 are not equal. Three smaller boxes do not automatically match two bigger ones.
The winner is right but the gap is not: 800 - 720 = 80, not 160.
level3.explanation: One large box is 8 x 3 x 10 = 240, so three hold 240 x 3 = 720 cubic inches. One jumbo box is 10 x 4 x 10 = 400, so two hold 400 x 2 = 800 cubic inches. 800 - 720 = 80, so the jumbo boxes give 80 cubic inches more for the same price.
hints: Find the volume of ONE box of each kind before comparing.
Large: 8 x 3 x 10 = 240. Jumbo: 10 x 4 x 10 = 400.
Now scale each to what you actually buy: 240 x 3 against 400 x 2, then subtract.
level3.stemEs: Una caja grande de cereal mide 8 por 3 por 10 pulgadas y una caja jumbo mide 10 por 4 por 10. Tres cajas grandes cuestan lo mismo que dos jumbo. ¿Cuál opción da MÁS cereal, y por cuánto?
choicesEs: Dos cajas jumbo, por 80 pulgadas cúbicas
Tres cajas grandes, por 80 pulgadas cúbicas
Dos cajas jumbo, por 160 pulgadas cúbicas
level3.explanationEs: Una caja grande es 8 x 3 x 10 = 240, y tres tienen 720. Una jumbo es 10 x 4 x 10 = 400, y dos tienen 800. 800 - 720 = 80.
hintsEs: Encuentra el volumen de UNA caja de cada tipo antes de comparar.
Grande: 8 x 3 x 10 = 240. Jumbo: 10 x 4 x 10 = 400.
Ahora ajusta a lo que compras: 240 x 3 contra 400 x 2, y luego resta.

level3.stem: A change jar holds pennies, nickels, dimes and quarters worth $53.50 in all. Why does the number of PENNIES have to be a multiple of 5?
choices: Because nickels, dimes and quarters all end in 0 or 5 cents, so only the pennies can make the total end in 0 — and it takes a multiple of 5 pennies to do that
Because $53.50 divided by 5 is a whole number
Because there are 5 pennies in a nickel
Because every jar of coins has a multiple of 5 pennies
choiceFeedback: That is true about the number 53.50, but it says nothing about which coins made it. The argument has to be about the coin values.
That is a fact about nickels, not a reason about the total. It does not explain why the total forces this.
A generalization needs a reason. Change the total to $53.53 and it stops being true.
level3.explanation: This is the generalization from Lesson 1-5. Every nickel, dime and quarter contributes a number of cents ending in 0 or 5. The total, $53.50, ends in 0. So the pennies must contribute an amount ending in 0 or 5 as well — and pennies are worth 1 cent each, so their COUNT has to be a multiple of 5.
hints: Think about the last digit each coin can contribute in cents.
A nickel is 5c, a dime 10c, a quarter 25c — every one of those ends in 0 or 5.
The total ends in 0. If the other coins can only end in 0 or 5, what must the pennies supply?
level3.stemEs: Un frasco de monedas tiene centavos, monedas de 5, de 10 y de 25, con un valor total de $53.50. ¿Por qué el número de CENTAVOS tiene que ser un múltiplo de 5?
choicesEs: Porque las monedas de 5, 10 y 25 terminan en 0 o en 5 centavos, así que solo los centavos pueden hacer que el total termine en 0, y para eso hace falta un múltiplo de 5
Porque $53.50 entre 5 da un número entero
Porque hay 5 centavos en una moneda de 5
Porque todo frasco de monedas tiene un múltiplo de 5 centavos
level3.explanationEs: Cada moneda de 5, 10 y 25 aporta centavos que terminan en 0 o en 5. El total, $53.50, termina en 0, así que los centavos deben aportar una cantidad que termine en 0 o 5, y valen 1 centavo cada uno.
hintsEs: Piensa en el último dígito que puede aportar cada moneda en centavos.
5c, 10c y 25c: todas terminan en 0 o en 5.
El total termina en 0. ¿Si las demás solo pueden terminar en 0 o 5, que deben aportar los centavos?

level3.stem: A recipe needs 0.75 of a 40-ounce bag of flour. How many ounces does the recipe need?
choiceFeedback: That adds 0.75 to 40. 'Of' a quantity means multiply, not add.
That divides 40 by 0.75. Dividing by a number less than 1 makes the result BIGGER than 40, but a part of the bag has to be smaller.
That misplaces the decimal. 0.75 of 40 is close to three quarters of 40, which is close to 30, not to 3.
level3.explanation: 0.75 is the same as three fourths, so this is 3/4 of 40. One fourth of 40 is 10, so three fourths is 3 x 10 = 30 ounces. Decimals and fractions are two ways of writing the same amount.
hints: Rewrite 0.75 as a fraction you recognise.
0.75 is three fourths. One fourth of 40 is 10.
Three fourths of 40 is 3 x 10.
level3.stemEs: Una receta necesita 0.75 de una bolsa de harina de 40 onzas. ¿Cuántas onzas necesita la receta?
level3.explanationEs: 0.75 es lo mismo que tres cuartos, así que esto es 3/4 de 40. Un cuarto de 40 es 10, y tres cuartos son 3 x 10 = 30 onzas.
hintsEs: Reescribe 0.75 como una fracción que reconozcas.
0.75 son tres cuartos. Un cuarto de 40 es 10.
Tres cuartos de 40 son 3 x 10.

level3.stem: Two patterns start at 0. Pattern A follows ADD 3 and pattern B follows ADD 9. Which statement about the two patterns is true for EVERY step?
choices: Each term of pattern B is 3 times the matching term of pattern A
Each term of pattern B is 6 more than the matching term of pattern A
Pattern B is 3 times pattern A only at the first step
The two patterns meet again after several steps
choiceFeedback: That holds at the second pair (9 - 3 = 6) and nowhere else: the next pair gives 18 - 6 = 12. A rule has to hold every time, not once.
It holds at every step, not just the first — write out four terms of each and compare.
They share only the starting 0. After that B pulls ahead and never comes back.
level3.explanation: Line them up. A: 0, 3, 6, 9, 12. B: 0, 9, 18, 27, 36. At every step, B is A times 3 — because B adds 3 times as much each step and both started at 0. A generalization has to hold for every term, not just the one you checked.
hints: Write out the first five terms of each pattern before deciding.
Compare them pair by pair. Is 9 three times 3? Is 18 three times 6?
level3.stemEs: Dos patrones empiezan en 0. El patrón A sigue SUMAR 3 y el patrón B sigue SUMAR 9. ¿Cuál afirmación sobre los dos patrones es cierta en CADA paso?
choicesEs: Cada término del patrón B es 3 veces el término correspondiente del patrón A
Cada término del patrón B es 6 más que el término correspondiente del patrón A
El patrón B es 3 veces el patrón A solo en el primer paso
Los dos patrones se vuelven a encontrar después de varios pasos
level3.explanationEs: Alinéalos. A: 0, 3, 6, 9, 12. B: 0, 9, 18, 27, 36. En cada paso, B es A por 3. Una generalización debe cumplirse en cada término.
hintsEs: Escribe los primeros cinco términos de cada patrón antes de decidir.
Compáralos por pares.¿Es 9 tres veces 3? ¿Es 18 tres veces 6?

level3.stem: A pile of coins is too big to count. You count one small stack: about 10 coins. About 15 stacks like that make the pile. A classmate says "so there are exactly 150 coins." What is wrong with saying EXACTLY?
choices: Both numbers were estimates, so the answer is about 150 — close enough to be useful, but not exact
Nothing is wrong; 15 x 10 is exactly 150
The multiplication is wrong, so the total cannot be 150
You should have counted every coin instead of estimating
choiceFeedback: The multiplication is exact, but the two numbers multiplied were both estimates, so the result is an estimate too.
15 x 10 = 150 is correct arithmetic. The problem is the word 'exactly', not the calculation.
Estimating was the right move — the pile is too big to count. The fix is to report the answer as 'about 150'.
level3.explanation: This is the estimate from Lesson 1-3. The arithmetic 15 x 10 = 150 is exact, but the numbers going IN were not: about 10 coins per stack, about 15 stacks. An estimate is a reasoned answer that is close enough to be useful — reporting it as exact claims more than the method can support.
hints: Were the two numbers you multiplied counted, or estimated?
About 10 per stack, and about 15 stacks. Neither was exact.
If what goes in is approximate, what comes out is approximate too.
level3.stemEs: Una pila de monedas es demasiado grande para contarla. Cuentas una pila pequeña: unas 10 monedas. Unas 15 pilas así forman el montón. Un compañero dice "entonces hay exactamente 150 monedas.¿" Qué está mal con decir EXACTAMENTE?
choicesEs: Los dos números eran estimaciones, así que la respuesta es unas 150: suficientemente cerca para ser útil, pero no exacta
No hay nada mal; 15 x 10 es exactamente 150
La multiplicación está mal, así que el total no puede ser 150
Debiste contar cada moneda en vez de estimar
level3.explanationEs: La aritmética 15 x 10 = 150 es exacta, pero los números que entraron no lo eran: unas 10 monedas por pila, unas 15 pilas. Una estimación es una respuesta razonada, suficientemente cerca para ser útil.
hintsEs: ¿Los dos números que multiplicaste, se contaron o se estimaron?
Unas 10 por pila y unas 15 pilas. Ninguno era exacto.
Si lo que entra es aproximado, lo que sale también lo es.
